questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Living in a fool’s paradise
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Living in a fool’s paradise

options.text: To believe wrongly that your situation is good
options.html: To believe wrongly that your situation is good

options.text: To live in luxuriously after fooling someone
options.html: To live in luxuriously after fooling someone

questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is To believe wrongly that your situation is good.
Key Points 

  • Let's look at the meaning of the given idiom:-
  • Living in a fool’s paradise - to believe wrongly and stupidly that your situation is good when really it is not. (गलत और मूर्खता से विश्वास करना कि आपकी स्थिति अच्छी है जबकि वास्तव में ऐसा नहीं है)

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. On tenterhooks
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

On tenterhooks
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Very tense.'

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: On tenterhooks means very tense, excited, or anxious about what might happen. (बहुत तनावपूर्ण)
    • Example: We were on tenterhooks all through the game, hoping against hope that our team would win.
  • From the given options, the second option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
     

Hence, the correct answer is option 2.

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "On tenterhooks" that it is all about a hook used to fasten cloth on a drying frame or tenter.
     

Additional Information

  • A tenter is a framework on which fabric can be held taut for drying or other treatment during the manufacturing process; in the past tenterhooks were hooks or bent nails fixed in the tenter to hold the fabric in position. The metaphorical use of the phrase for an agitated state of mind dates from the mid 18th century.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence. He is very impulsive and does things without rhyme or reason .
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.

He is very impulsive and does things without rhyme or reason.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'without a reasonable explanation.'
Key Points
  • If we read the sentence, we get to know that the person is impulsive and he does things .... (in a negative manner)
  • The phrase 'without rhyme or reason' means without any obvious reasonable explanation. (बिना किसी स्पष्ट उचित स्पष्टीकरण के)
    • He was sent behind the bars without rhyme or reason.
  • Hence, the correct answer is option 4.
Additional Information
  • The phrase 'rhyme or reason' means sense, logic, meaning, or planning.
  • And when we add 'without or with no' in the beginning, it becomes without any obvious reasonable explanation.
    • We will have to repent if we do something without rhyme or reason.

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. To fish in troubled waters
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To fish in troubled waters

options.text: To take advantage of a difficult situation.
options.html: To take advantage of a difficult situation.

options.text: To try to do something that is very difficult.
options.html: To try to do something that is very difficult.

options.text: To catch fish in stormy weather in the sea.
options.html: To catch fish in stormy weather in the sea.

options.text: To try to find a big catch in the deep sea.
options.html: To try to find a big catch in the deep sea.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'To take advantage of a difficult situation.'

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: To fish in troubled waters means to try to take advantage of a difficult or confusing situation. (किसी कठिन या भ्रमित करने वाली स्थिति का लाभ उठाने का प्रयास करना)
    • Example: Stay away from those who try to fish in troubled waters.
  • From the given options, the first option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
     

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "To fish in troubled waters" that it is all about catching fish in stormy weather in the sea.
     

Additional Information

  • This term, first recorded in 1568, expresses the even older notion that fish bite more readily when seas are rough.

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. A dime a dozen

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Made out of whole cloth
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Made out of whole cloth
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Entirely false and fabricated'.

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: Made out of whole cloth means completely fabricated and not based on reality at all.
    • Example: This report is positively denied in official circles, who affirm that nothing of the kind occurred, but that the story is made out of whole cloth.
  • From the given options, the third option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
     

Hence, the correct answer is option 3.

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "Made out of whole cloth" that it is all about something made out of the cloth, but the correct answer is option 3. So be careful while dealing with such questions.
     

Additional Information

  • In the 15th century, this expression referred to something fabricated from cloth that ran the full length of the loom. However, by the 1800s it was common practice for tailors to deceive their customers and, instead of using whole cloth, actually make garments from pieced goods. Their advertising slogan, "cut out of whole cloth," thus came to mean "made up, false."

  • Reinventing the wheel: to waste time learning how to do something when it is already known how to do it

    ​

Correct Sentence: Wasting one's time for things that have already been satisfactorily done. 

Additional Information

  • Let's look at some idioms the word 'Get' are:
  • Idiom Meaning Example
    Get socked with something to suddenly receive something that causes you problems (अचानक कुछ प्राप्त करने के लिए जो आपको परेशान करता है) If you don't pay your credit card bill on time, you'll get socked with a huge late fee.
    Get someone's wires crossed to have a different understanding of the same situation (एक ही स्थिति की एक अलग समझ रखने के लिए) We must have got our wires crossed – I thought she was arriving tomorrow, not today.
    Get something out of your system to do something enough so that you do not want to do it any longer(इतना कुछ करने के लिए कि आप इसे अब और नहीं करना चाहते हैं) Let the kids run around a little longer, maybe they’ll get it out of their system.

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Neither fish nor fowl
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Neither fish nor fowl

options.text: Something which can neither be purchased nor be grown
options.html: Something which can neither be purchased nor be grown

options.text: Something which can neither be supplied easily nor be made available readily
options.html: Something which can neither be supplied easily nor be made available readily

options.text: Something which can neither be categorized easily nor be accepted befittingly
options.html: Something which can neither be categorized easily nor be accepted befittingly

options.text: Something which can neither be eaten nor be preserved
options.html: Something which can neither be eaten nor be preserved

questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Something which can neither be categorized easily nor be accepted befittingly'.

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: Neither fish nor fowl means something or someone which is not easily categorized; something or someone that does not rightly belong or fit well in a given group or situation.
    • Example: Graduate teaching assistants are neither fish nor fowl, neither completely students nor teachers.
  • From the given options, the third option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
     

Hence, the correct answer is option 3.

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "Neither fish nor fowl" that it is all about a fish or fowl, but the correct answer is option 3. So be careful while dealing with such questions.
     

Additional Information

  • According to the Oxford Dictionary of English Idioms, this idiom derives from dietary laws of the church, having to do with abstaining from certain foods or fasting. The original meaning of the idiom referred to something that was not fit for any class of people, or not fit for one thing or the other.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Parthian shot
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Parthian shot
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Parting hit'. 

Key Points

  • The most appropriate meaning of the given idiom is 'Parting hit'. 
  • Parthian shot: Parting hit is another term for 'Parting hit'. The meaning of it is: a remark that you make when you are leaving so that it has a stronger effect
    • Example: In a Parthian shot, the departing president is wrapping himself in a spurious mantle of civil liberty. 
  • By reading the above explanation we find that the correct answer is Option 1. 
    ​

Correct Answer: Parting hit. 

Additional Information

  • The story behind the idiom 'Parthian Shot' as follows: 
    • The Parthian shot is a light horse military tactic made famous by the Parthians, an ancient Iranian people.
    • While being in real or feigned retreat, their horse archers would turn their bodies back in full gallop to shoot at the pursuing enemy.
    • The maneuver required superb equestrian skills since the rider's hands were occupied by his composite bow.
    • As the stirrup had not been invented at the time of the Parthians, the rider relied solely on pressure from his legs to guide his horse.

Key Points

  • The given sentence is an idiom. An idiom is a group of words established by usage as having a meaning not deducible from those of the individual words (e.g. over the moon, see the light ).
  • Given Idiom: Flying off the handle means to become suddenly enraged.
    • For example, Linda called me back and apologized for flying off the handle.
       

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "Flying off the handle" that it is all about flying away, being launched from a handle, but the correct answer is option 1. So be careful while dealing with such questions.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Look before you leap

questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Think carefully of the consequences'. 

Key Points

  • The most appropriate word of the given idiom is 'Think carefully of the consequences'. 
  • Look before you leap: Think of the consequences before you act. 
    • Example: You better check out the costs that you will have to incur through the duration of this lawsuit before filling it. It is always better to look before you leap. 
  • Therefore, by reading the above explanation we find that the correct answer is Option 2. 
    ​

Correct Answer: Think carefully of the consequences. 

Additional Information 

  • The other idioms of the word 'Look' as follows:
    • Look someone in the eye: to talk to someone in an honest way that shows no doubts
      • Example: I wanted to look people in the eye and tell them I made a mistake.
    • Look right through someone: to pretend not to see someone even while your eyes are directed toward that person
      • Example: I smiled at him, but he looked right through me.
    • Looking for trouble: behaving in a way that is likely to cause problems for you
      • Example: Parking illegally in front of the police station is looking for trouble.

​

  • Look before you leap: बिना विचारे जो करे, सो पाछे पछताय

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Make a beeline

Make a beeline
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Go straight to.'

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: Make a beeline means to go straight to somebody or something.

Mistake Points

The correct answer is- To be the last in a series of events leading one to feel that it is intolerable​​.

Key Points

  • Let's look at the meaning of the given idiom:
    • The straw that broke the camel’s back- the last in a series of bad things that happen to make someone very upset, angry, etc
  • Example: 
    • It had been a difficult week, so when the car broke down, it was the straw that broke the camel's back.
       

​ ​​​​Additional Information  

  • Let's look at the origin of the idiom:
    • According to Wikipedia, the straw that broke the camel's back is from an Arabic proverb about “how a camel is loaded beyond its capacity to move or stand”.
    • It is a "reference to any process by which cataclysmic failure (a broken back) is achieved by a seemingly inconsequential addition, a single straw."
